readme.text:
# [Phishing Support](https://phishing.support/)

Phishing Support is an open-source tool to help automate the analysis, reporting, and tracking of phishing emails and malicious websites. It extracts indicators (links, domains, sender headers), performs quick automated checks, and helps to takedown by reporting it to the appropriate providers.

## Goal

- Make it easy to inspect suspicious emails and websites.
- Automate repetitive abuse-reporting tasks.
- Provide a privacy-conscious, auditable record of reports and analysis.

## Features

- Parse and analyze `.eml` email files and extract useful metadata and links.
- Quick automated classification (e.g., likely phishing / probably safe).
- Helpers to report phishing websites to hosting providers, registrars, and takedown services.
- Web UI for submitting emails and URLs, and for reviewing saved reports.

## Quick demo

1. Forward a phishing email to `report@phishing.support` or upload an `.eml` file via the [web UI](https://phishing.support/).
2. Paste a suspicious website URL into the Website field and click Report.
3. The app extracts indicators, performs automated checks, and attempts to report the issue.

## Abuse-report reply correspondence

SMTP abuse reports are stored as individual correspondence threads. Each report uses the configured, authenticated `SMTP_FROM` address as its visible `From` address and a new opaque `Reply-To` address such as `case-<32 hexadecimal characters>@phishing.support`. The reply identity is random, does not contain a submission ID, and is unique to one report target.

Before enabling SMTP report delivery, configure inbound mail for the reply domain:

- Set `REPORT_REPLY_DOMAIN=phishing.support` and keep it equal to the domain in `IMAP_LISTEN_ADDRESS` (for example, `report@phishing.support`). The listener rejects a mismatch at startup.
- Keep `SMTP_FROM` as a real, authenticated mailbox in the SMTP provider. Generated identities are only `Reply-To` addresses; they are never used as `From` or as the SMTP envelope sender.
- For iCloud Custom Email Domain, enable **Allow All Incoming Emails** for `phishing.support`. This catch-all must deliver to the mailbox configured by `IMAP_MAILBOX`; confirm the mailbox/rules before rollout. See Apple’s [catch-all configuration guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/icloud/allow-all-incoming-emails-mm9e3ee0680f/icloud).
- Configure `IMAP_HOST`, `IMAP_PORT`, `IMAP_SECURE`, `IMAP_USER`, `IMAP_PASS`, `IMAP_MAILBOX`, and `IMAP_LISTEN_ADDRESS` for that monitored mailbox.
- Perform a controlled preflight: send one report to a test recipient, reply to its generated `Reply-To`, and verify both messages and attachments appear in the submission’s Reports tab.

Incoming mail is assigned only by an exact generated recipient address, an exact outbound RFC `Message-ID` in `In-Reply-To`/`References`, or a unique diagnostic thread header. The listener never guesses from sender, subject, or quoted content. Forwarded messages to `report@phishing.support` continue through the normal submission intake path. Other messages are recorded as ignored in the IMAP ledger, marked read, and left in the mailbox.

Do not substitute plus-addressing if catch-all routing is unavailable. Use a dedicated reply subdomain backed by a catch-all-capable inbound provider while retaining the authenticated SMTP sender.

## Supplemental Netcraft reporting

Every standalone abuse report with one or more validated observed URLs creates an independent Netcraft Reporting API v3 submission route. This happens alongside normal resolver-selected provider routes and the existing eligible Google Safe Browsing supplemental route. Netcraft receives every observed URL associated with a target in one API submission; the returned submission UUID is retained with the report for auditability.

Every email confirmed as phishing is also sent to Netcraft's documented `POST /report/mail` endpoint using the original submitted RFC 822/MIME source. The original source is retained as the submission artifact and linked to the Netcraft report. Netcraft accepts messages up to 20 MiB; larger messages are recorded as a local failed report and are never sent. A durable pre-call marker prevents an interrupted or ambiguous request from being replayed automatically, while explicit API rejections remain visible as failed reports.

Netcraft's API requires a reporter email. The service uses `ABUSE_NETCRAFT_REPORTER_EMAIL`, which defaults to `support@phishing.support` in Docker deployments. It deliberately does not disclose an optional public reporter contact email. URL-only providers are not given invented URLs: a target without a validated observed URL remains eligible for its resolver-derived abuse routes, but has no Netcraft or Google Safe Browsing supplemental submission to make.

## Privacy note

Only submit emails or links that you are allowed to share publicly. The project is intended to help protect users and organizations - do not use it to probe private systems or to impersonate abuse inquiries.

## Contributing

Contributions, bug reports, and improvements are welcome. Please open issues or pull requests on the project's repository. When contributing, keep changes focused and include tests where appropriate.

# WPlace - World Archive

## Map: [wplace.samuelscheit.com](https://wplace.samuelscheit.com/)

A project to scrape, archive and visualize the entire https://wplace.live map.

The map is divided into 2048x2048 tiles, each with a dimension of 1000x1000 pixels.
Each base tile is stored as a PNG file in `public/tiles/11` during archive generation, then `scripts/vips.py` builds the lower zoom levels.
Full-world archiving runs on the self-hosted Linux runner with IPv6 freebind.

## Setup

1. Clone the repository
2. Install dependencies with `npm install`
3. Run a small local archive test with `npm run archive:world -- --start-x=0 --start-y=0 --width=1 --height=1 --out=/tmp/wplace-tiles --clean=true --rps=1 --concurrency=1`
4. For full-world CI runs, set the `WPLACE_IPV6_SUBNET` secret to the routed IPv6 subnet on the self-hosted runner.

pullRequests.title: fix: discard npm-modified package-lock.json before git pull in self-hosted workflows
pullRequests.body:
`npm install` modifies `package-lock.json`, leaving uncommitted local changes that cause `git pull --no-rebase` to abort with a merge conflict before the `snapshots.json` update can be pushed.

## Changes

- **Both `map-selfhosted-linux.yml` and `map-selfhosted-mac.yml`**: add `git restore package-lock.json` after committing `snapshots.json` and before `git pull`, discarding the `npm install` side-effect so the pull proceeds cleanly.

```diff
  git commit -m "Update snapshots.json [skip ci]"
+ git restore package-lock.json
  git config pull.rebase false
  git pull
  git push
```

Get the sources with `git clone https://github.com/SamuelScheit/wahllage/` 2. Change into the directory with `cd wahllage` 3. Install the JavaScript runtime and toolkit [Bun](https://bun.sh/) a) Without the install script, it would be `npm install bun` and `export PATH=/path/to/wahllage/node_modules/.bin/:$PATH` 4. Install the dependencies with `bun install` (in some installs it is `bun.exe`) Scraper code now lives under `src/lib/scraper/`. Provider entry points can be run directly, e.g. bun src/lib/scraper/providers/bundeslaender/sachsen.ts or bun src/lib/scraper/providers/krzn.ts Results are merged into `src/lib/scraper/cache/wahlbezirkeList.json` via `saveResults`.

## CODEBASE SLOP RATIO: 75%

# new_harness

Minimal Codex-style harness target:

- Ratatui UI.
- Responses API over WebSocket.
- WebSocket connections are pooled and kept open instead of repeatedly reconnecting.
- New WebSocket handshakes are rate-limited to 60 per minute.
- Native in-process subagents.
- Native Responses tool specs. The CLI advertises freeform `locate`, `read_file`, `edit_file`,
  `terminal_open`, `terminal_write`, and `terminal_read`; root turns persist tool outputs before
  continuation requests.
- `locate`: get context. If know nothing, ask
  directly: `need context for [your task]`. If enough known, ask specific: `how thing1 implemented`,
  `what is /path/file`, `all data structures for feature`, or `how edit_file implemented`.
  Locator tool no omniscient; pass semantically required info for good result. Get context only; do
  not ask locator to make decisions. `read_file` emits compact line-boundary anchors. `edit_file`
  applies native anchor-based edits directly.
- Manual compaction.
- Steering prompts: queue for the next tool boundary, or interrupt and send immediately.

This workspace intentionally excludes app-server, MCP/apps/connectors, plugin/skill systems, cloud
tasks, memories, external-agent migration, and provider-specific local model integrations.

## Native ChatGPT web provider

The harness embeds `headless-api-client` directly in `harness-chatgpt-web-transport`; no loopback bridge or browser-controller sidecar is required for normal startup. The transport restores the durable native cookie/session snapshot in-process and validates it through the recovered session lifecycle. If that session has expired, the optional passkey file is consulted lazily and the same native FIDO2 + AAS flow reauthenticates before the model transport becomes ready.

The transport runs the exact account/conversation typestates on one dedicated current-thread worker. The worker exclusively owns native transport, integrity/Sentinel state, and conversation authority; harness tasks exchange immutable commands and model events with it rather than sharing mutable protocol objects.
Add a profile like this to the harness state directory's `providers.json` (replace the model slug and local context-window metadata with the values you want the harness to use for compaction/accounting):

```json
{
  "default_profile_id": "chatgpt-web",
  "profiles": [
    {
      "id": "chatgpt-web",
      "display_name": "ChatGPT Web",
      "kind": "chatgpt-web",
      "auth": null,
      "driver": {
        "type": "chatgpt-web",
        "session_file": "/home/me/.local/share/chatgpt-headless/session.json",
        "passkey_file": "/home/me/.config/chatgpt-headless/passkey.json",
        "timezone_offset_min": 0,
        "stream_idle_timeout_ms": 60000,
        "native_tools": {
          "system_hints": [],
          "connector_ids": ["CHATGPT_MCP_CONNECTOR_ID"],
          "mcp_enabled_tools": ["box_list", "inspect", "edit_file"],
          "disabled_tool_ids": [],
          "local_function_names": []
        }
      },
      "default_model": "MODEL_SLUG",
      "default_reasoning_effort": null,
      "default_service_tier": null,
      "model_configs": [
        {
          "slug": "MODEL_SLUG",
          "context_window": 128000,
          "effective_context_window_percent": 90,
          "supports_tools": false,
          "supports_parallel_tool_calls": false
        }
      ],
      "tool_output_summary_model": null,
      "developer_role_support": "supported",
      "supports_freeform_tool_input": false
    }
  ]
}
```

`native_tools` configures capabilities already known to the ChatGPT backend/client. `system_hints` selects native ChatGPT modes/capabilities, while `connector_ids` contains raw ChatGPT connector ids. The in-process transport encodes each connector id with the recovered web-client rule `connector:<id>` and places it in the ordinary `system_hints` request field. The backend-produced `selected_mcp_sources` message metadata is intentionally not synthesized by the client. `disabled_tool_ids` suppresses backend-known tools. Harness tools are registered once through the real ChatGPT MCP connector; browser-host local functions are neither synthesized nor used.

`mcp_enabled_tools` is an exact allow-list for the harness's `codex-native-mcp` server, not conversation metadata. When `codex-native-mcp` starts it discovers the same harness-state `providers.json` and applies the default ChatGPT-web profile; `--provider-config <path>` and `--provider-profile <id>` select an explicit shared config/profile. The allow-list is enforced independently in both MCP `tools/list` and `tools/call`. Omit the field for backward-compatible allow-all behavior; an explicit empty array exposes no MCP tools. The ChatGPT connector itself still needs to be created/connected once through ChatGPT and its resulting connector id placed in `connector_ids`. A running MCP endpoint has one active allow-list, so distinct ChatGPT-web profiles that need different tool policies should use separate `codex-native-mcp --provider-profile ...` instances (and therefore separate registered ChatGPT connector ids/endpoints).

Harness system/developer instructions remain separate from ChatGPT's backend-owned system prompt. On the first native conversation turn they are sent as a hidden `developer` message; subsequent turns reuse the stateful backend conversation. A canonical-history rewrite currently returns `ReconnectRequired` instead of silently flattening or fabricating history. Model-attempt cancellation consumes the conversation typestate's one-shot stop authority, which uses ChatGPT's `/stop_conversation` path when the live conversation id is known and always aborts the local stream authority.

The ChatGPT-web transport continues to report `tool_calls = false` for provider-neutral harness tool schemas: those schemas are not serialized into the ChatGPT conversation request. Backend-native MCP instead runs through the selected ChatGPT `mcp_connector`, whose Streamable HTTP endpoint is `codex-native-mcp`; this preserves ChatGPT's native connector/tool execution path while letting the harness config choose which MCP tools the server exposes.

## Crates

- `harness-conversation-runtime`: conversation state machine and durable transitions.
- `harness-runtime-driver`: runtime-effect execution, model streaming, command gating, and tool deadlines.
- `harness-session-store` and `harness-session-service`: durable session contracts, manifest-backed
  immutable generations, discovery, and postcard/zstd encoding.

- `harness-tool-api` and `harness-tool-execution`: tool contracts and capability-rooted implementations.
- Model/provider protocol and transport crates isolate wire formats from runtime policy.
- `harness-tui-rewrite`: Ratatui rendering and input; `harness-cli`: composition and entrypoint.

## Runtime wiring

The TUI sends ordered runtime commands through the CLI composition layer. `ConversationRuntime`
validates each transition and produces `RuntimeEffect` values. `harness-runtime-driver` executes those
effects against the selected model transport and tool executor, then emits ordered runtime events back
to the TUI. Durable transitions remain owned by the session store behind the runtime.

```text
TUI -> RuntimeCommand -> ConversationRuntime -> RuntimeEffect -> RuntimeDriver
                                                           \-> ModelTransport
                                                           \-> ToolExecutor
                                                           \-> SessionStore
```

Session storage is manifest-backed. Each session directory contains immutable postcard/zstd
compaction segments and framed journal generations; only the journal named by the final manifest
entry is appendable. Normal appends compress only their new record batch. A runtime compaction
writes its already-materialized replacement checkpoint to a new immutable segment, creates the next
empty journal, and atomically replaces the small postcard manifest. Writer close only flushes the
active journal; it never reloads or recompresses prior history. Startup accepts the complete prefix
of the active journal after a crash, while older manifest entries remain immutable.


CLI-created root session/thread ids are UUID-shaped strings, and durable lookup is scoped to the
workspace-specific session directory.

WebSocket sockets themselves are not durable. The durable WS pool state stores only the next
allowed new-connection timestamp. Normal operation reuses completed idle sockets within the same
provider/auth pool; request-specific Codex headers do not partition idle sockets. Current per-frame
metadata such as window id, parent thread id, subagent, installation id, and turn metadata is
stamped into each WebSocket request body. Cold handshakes are spaced by 1500ms by default.
Automatic startup prewarm is not wired by default; sockets are opened on demand unless a caller
explicitly sends a prewarm request.

## MCP server

The primary operator workflow is interactive:

```sh
codex-native-mcp
```

When attached to a terminal, that opens the MCP manager instead of immediately starting a server.
On first use it asks where to create the catalog, then guides box creation through project path,
access, and execution choices. No TOML editing is required.

A typical first run is:

1. Choose a project-local `.harness/boxes.toml` or the user catalog.
2. Choose **Add box** and accept the current project defaults.
3. Choose **Start MCP server**.
4. Use the printed loopback endpoint, normally `http://127.0.0.1:8472/mcp`.
5. Expose that endpoint through HTTPS before adding it to ChatGPT.

The server stays running while the terminal becomes a live operator console. From that console you
can list, add, edit, or remove boxes, open the catalog in `$VISUAL`/`$EDITOR`, and reload manually.
Successful changes are published to new MCP requests without changing the HTTP port or interrupting
in-flight tool calls. External file edits are also detected automatically within about one second.
Invalid edits are logged once and the last working registry continues serving.

Every guided save validates the exact generated TOML and opens the complete MCP registry before it
is accepted. The previous file is retained as `<catalog>.bak`. The manager writes normalized TOML;
manual comments remain available in the backup when a guided edit rewrites the file.

Direct commands expose the same operations:

```sh
codex-native-mcp add [box-id]
codex-native-mcp edit [box-id]
codex-native-mcp remove [box-id]
codex-native-mcp show [box-id]
codex-native-mcp boxes
codex-native-mcp check
```

`check` opens every workspace and validates the aggregated MCP tool contracts without starting lazy
sandbox processes. Catalog discovery is shared with `new_harness`, in this order:

1. `--catalog <path>`.
2. `HARNESS_BOXES`.
3. The nearest `.harness/boxes.toml` while walking upward from the current directory.
4. `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/new_harness/boxes.toml`, or `$HOME/.config/new_harness/boxes.toml`.
5. The legacy `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/codex-native-mcp/boxes.toml` location.

For an unattended foreground service, specify `serve`. Redirected stdin/stdout also preserves the
old no-command service behavior:

```sh
export CODEX_NATIVE_MCP_PASSWORD='choose-a-password'
codex-native-mcp serve
```

The interactive manager uses `CODEX_NATIVE_MCP_PASSWORD` when present. Otherwise it can generate a
consent password for that process and prints it once before startup. `--no-auth` is available for
loopback testing. Port `0` asks the operating system for an available loopback port and the actual
endpoint is printed after binding.

Expose the printed loopback endpoint through HTTPS, for example:

```sh
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8472
```

Append `/mcp` to the resulting HTTPS tunnel URL when adding the connector to ChatGPT.

### Standalone Responses proxy and Secure MCP Tunnel

`proxy` replaces the previous public-URL connector registration and manual
bridge commands. It is the only supported path for a local Codex-compatible
Responses WebSocket endpoint: it restores or creates a ChatGPT session, starts
the loopback MCP relay and embedded OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel, creates or
reuses the tunnel-backed ChatGPT connector, and persists the resolved IDs.

The tunnel exposes one stable `codex_client_tool` MCP action. It is a relay,
not an executor: on each Responses turn the proxy records the actual function
and freeform tools declared by the connected Codex client. When ChatGPT calls
the tunnel action, the proxy emits that exact tool call back to the same Codex
client. The client executes it under its own current working directory,
sandbox, approval policy, writable roots, and tool runtime, then returns the
tool result through the proxy. The proxy never selects a Harness box or runs a
workspace command for this path.

The tunnel-facing action remains deliberately annotated
`readOnlyHint=true`, `destructiveHint=false`, `idempotentHint=true`, and
`openWorldHint=false`, as required for temporary ChatGPT connector metadata.
Those annotations do not replace the connected Codex client's actual policy;
the client remains authoritative for whether an operation may execute.

Log in once, then start the proxy:

```sh
cargo run -p headless-api-client --bin proxy -- \
  login --passkey-json /path/to/passkey-credential.json

CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY='runtime-tunnel-key' \
cargo run -p headless-api-client --bin proxy --
```

On the first run with no saved/discoverable tunnel, add a tunnel-management key
with **Tunnels Read + Manage** permission. The proxy derives the ChatGPT
workspace association from the authenticated session; no tunnel or connector
ID is entered manually:

```sh
CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY='runtime-tunnel-key' \
CHATGPT_PROXY_TUNNEL_ADMIN_KEY='tunnel-admin-key' \
cargo run -p headless-api-client --bin proxy --
```

It prints and saves `tunnel_id` and `connector_id` in
`~/.local/share/headless-api-client/proxy.json` (use `--state-file` or
`CHATGPT_PROXY_STATE_FILE` to relocate it). The default WebSocket endpoint is
`ws://127.0.0.1:43126/v1/responses`, configurable through `--port` or
`CHATGPT_PROXY_PORT`. The embedded MCP relay listens only on `127.0.0.1:8080`;
the tunnel is outbound-only and exposes no public ingress. A non-loopback
Responses listener requires `--api-key` or `CHATGPT_PROXY_API_KEY`.

The public Responses endpoint, embedded MCP endpoint, and Secure MCP Tunnel
control-plane client append every HTTP request/response and every Responses
WebSocket frame to
`~/.local/share/headless-api-client/requests.log` by default. Records carry a
shared exchange ID and preserve raw headers, query strings, and body bytes;
they are deliberately **not redacted** so protocol and provider failures can be
reconstructed exactly. Set `HARNESS_REQUEST_LOG_FILE` (or the compatibility
aliases `CHATGPT_PROXY_LOG_FILE` / `CODEX_NATIVE_MCP_LOG_FILE`) to use another
path. The file is created owner-only (`0600`) and is flushed after each record,
but it contains credentials, OAuth codes, and user/tool content—treat it as
highly sensitive and do not upload it unchanged. Standalone
`codex-native-mcp` uses the same logger and environment variables.

The proxy uses a temporary ChatGPT conversation by default. It sets ChatGPT's
`history_and_training_disabled` and `is_do_not_remember` request flags on every
native turn, so the conversation is not retained as a normal chat. Use `--persistent-chat` (or
`CHATGPT_PROXY_TEMPORARY_CHAT=false`) to retain every turn;
`--temporary-chat` selects temporary mode explicitly.

ChatGPT probes the Go in-process MCP server carried by the Secure Tunnel, not
the loopback Rust HTTP endpoint directly. The Go server mirrors the stable
relay action and preserves its read-only metadata and explicit `outputSchema`.
Omitting that schema makes ChatGPT record `openai/outputSchemaMissing` and
classify the action as a write. On every proxy start, after the tunnel is live,
the proxy calls the recovered `/aip/connectors/mcp/refresh_actions` operation
for the connector's accessible link and polls until ChatGPT reports exactly the
expected relay action with normalized metadata (`is_read_only=true`,
`is_destructive=false`, `is_consequential=false`, and `is_open_world=false`).
This refresh is required for saved connector IDs, which otherwise can retain a
stale action catalogue or stale metadata.

Run `proxy --help` for all persistent-state, session, listen, tunnel, and
optional API-key controls. Go 1.26.2 or newer is required by the vendored
in-process OpenAI tunnel SDK; set `GO=/path/to/go` if it is not on `PATH`.

The standalone `codex-native-mcp` catalog service remains available when you
explicitly want its box-scoped `box_list`, `inspect`, `edit_file`, and terminal
tool set to execute directly on this host. The Responses proxy no longer uses
that catalog: its purpose is to preserve the authority of the connected Codex
client.

## Local harness

Required:

- Harness ChatGPT auth state at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/new_harness/auth.json`, or
  `$HOME/.local/state/new_harness/auth.json` when `XDG_STATE_HOME` is unset. If the harness state
  file does not exist, the CLI imports the current Codex access token from `$CODEX_HOME/auth.json`
  or `$HOME/.codex/auth.json`.
- Harness base instructions at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/new_harness/instructions.md`, or
  `$HOME/.local/state/new_harness/instructions.md` when `XDG_STATE_HOME` is unset.

### Start in the current project

Running without a box uses the current directory with unrestricted host execution:

```sh
new_harness
```

During development the equivalent is:

```sh
cargo run -p harness-cli --
```

This is an explicit `unrestricted` backend, not a sandbox fallback. File operations still resolve
through the pinned workspace capability, while terminals, Cargo, `which`, and process inspection run
with the harness user's normal host authority.

The status line identifies the binding on every screen, for example:

```text
box: new_harness · host/rw │ session: ...
```

Use `/box` inside the TUI to show the project path, execution mode, access, catalog, and scoped
session directory. The active box cannot change inside a conversation; start another harness process
to work in another box.

### Configure named boxes

A project-local catalog is the simplest setup:

```sh
mkdir -p .harness
cp examples/boxes.toml .harness/boxes.toml
new_harness boxes --check
```

Then start a named box directly:

```sh
new_harness @new-harness-host
new_harness @new-harness-readonly
```

The wordier equivalent `new_harness box new-harness-host` is also accepted. `--box <id>` remains
available for scripts.

Catalog discovery is shared by the local harness and MCP server, in this order:

1. `--catalog <path>` (legacy `--box-config` is also accepted by `new_harness`).
2. `HARNESS_BOXES`.
3. The nearest `.harness/boxes.toml` while walking upward from the current directory.
4. `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/new_harness/boxes.toml`, or `$HOME/.config/new_harness/boxes.toml`.
5. The legacy `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/codex-native-mcp/boxes.toml` location.

Use `new_harness boxes` to see which catalog was found and which projects it exposes. Add `--check`
to open every workspace and validate its mode without starting lazy sandbox processes.

The catalog schema is:

```toml
schema = 1

[[boxes]]
id = "project-host"
display_name = "Project on host"
description = "Normal development environment"

[boxes.project]
path = "/absolute/or/catalog-relative/project"
access = "read-write"

[boxes.execution]
kind = "unrestricted"
```

Execution modes are deliberately distinct:

- `unrestricted` runs processes directly on the host on every supported platform.
- `file-only` registers filesystem inspection, and registers `edit_file` only when project access is
  `read-write`; no terminal tools are registered.
- `sandboxed` is compiled only on Linux. It requires `root`, `dnf_cache`, and `launcher` paths,
  accepts an optional persistent `environment` table, and lazily starts one durable Fedora sandbox
  when that box first executes a process. On non-Linux systems, selecting a sandboxed box fails
  explicitly; it never degrades to unrestricted execution.

`examples/boxes.toml` contains runnable unrestricted and read-only boxes plus a commented Linux
sandbox template. Sandboxed roots are persistent mutable Fedora roots, so package changes made with
Fedora's own `dnf5` remain available across launches.

Sandbox commands use `/workspace` as `HOME`. Their default `PATH` includes
`/workspace/.cargo/bin` and `/workspace/.local/bin`, so tools installed by rustup, Cargo, pip, and
similar user-level installers remain available to later agent commands. Override or extend the
persistent environment per box when needed:

```toml
[boxes.execution.environment]
PATH = "/workspace/bin:/workspace/.cargo/bin:/workspace/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"
CARGO_HOME = "/workspace/.cargo"
RUSTUP_HOME = "/workspace/.rustup"
```

Sandboxed boxes may optionally define per-command and aggregate cgroup v2 limits:

```toml
[boxes.execution.cgroup]
memory_high = 6442450944
memory_max = 8589934592
memory_swap_max = 0
pids_max = 512
cpu_quota_micros = 400000
cpu_period_micros = 100000
```

The durable launcher is placed in a protected `service/` cgroup. The shared `jobs/` branch and every
`jobs/job-N/` leaf receive the configured limits, so one job and all concurrent jobs together are
bounded. `memory.oom.group=1` on each leaf makes a memory failure terminate the complete command,
not the namespace-holding launcher. Reaching `memory.max` or `pids.max` is reported as a typed
resource-limit result. When `memory_max` is present and `memory_swap_max` is omitted, swap defaults
to zero so the hard boundary cannot spill into unlimited host swap.

When `parent` is omitted, the delegated parent is derived from the current process. Start the MCP or
CLI in a systemd user unit with an empty delegated parent:

```ini
[Service]
Delegate=yes
DelegateSubgroup=supervisor
```

`DelegateSubgroup=supervisor` places the harness process below the unit root, satisfying cgroup v2's
no-internal-process rule. An explicit absolute `parent` may instead be configured inside
`[boxes.execution.cgroup]`. Opening a constrained box fails rather than silently running without
limits when the parent is not cgroup v2, contains internal processes, lacks the requested
controllers, or is not writable.

### Resume conversations

Sessions are scoped to the workspace binding. A session from one project or box is never offered by
`resume` in another project or box.

```sh
new_harness resume
new_harness @new-harness-host resume
new_harness @new-harness-host resume <session-id>
```

On exit, the CLI prints the complete command needed to reopen that conversation in the same box.
Changing the catalog file's location does not change the session scope; the box id, project, mode,
and access do.

Sessions created before workspace scoping remain available explicitly through
`new_harness legacy resume [session-id]`. This mode is labeled `[legacy]` in the status line and
cannot be combined with a named box or used to create a new session.

`HARNESS_SESSION_ROOT` overrides the base state directory. Workspace-specific session directories
are created beneath `<base>/workspaces/`; they are not pooled into one global `sessions/` directory.

### Shared box catalog

The local harness consumes the same catalog managed by `codex-native-mcp`. A box created or edited in
the MCP manager can be launched locally with `new_harness @<box>`. The catalog schema and execution
modes are therefore one shared product surface rather than separate MCP and local configurations.


Optional:

- `CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY='your-runtime-tunnel-key'`
- `CHATGPT_PROXY_TUNNEL_ADMIN_KEY='tunnel-admin-key-with-tunnels-read-and-manage'`
- `CODEX_HOME` selects the Codex auth directory.
- `XDG_STATE_HOME` selects the harness state directory.
- `HARNESS_BOXES` selects the shared box catalog.
- `HARNESS_MODEL` defaults to `gpt-5.5`.
- `HARNESS_REASONING_EFFORT` defaults to `xhigh`.
- `HARNESS_SERVICE_TIER` defaults to `fast` (`priority` on the wire).
- `OPENAI_BASE_URL` defaults to `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex`.
- `HARNESS_SESSION_ROOT` overrides the workspace-scoped session base directory.
- `--norotate` bypasses harness state and reads Codex `auth.json` only. Without `--norotate`, token
  refresh is only attempted when the harness state file contains a harness-owned refresh token; the
  default Codex import does not copy Codex's refresh token.

`WorkspaceContext` separates the pinned project capability from the selected process executor.
`edit_file` and filesystem inspection share one resolver; terminal sessions, process inspection,
and Cargo operations use exactly the box's explicit backend.

Phase 9 tool-shape experiment:

```sh
cargo run -p harness-cli -- experiment freeform-parallel --norotate
```

The experiment command uses the same ChatGPT/Codex auth path as the TUI, queries `/models`, then
runs live Responses WebSocket requests for two controlled custom/freeform tools and two comparable
function tools. It prints model metadata, the request `parallel_tool_calls` value, sent tool specs,
event order/item ids, inferred call overlap or serialization, continuation behavior, latency, and
token usage when the backend returns usage.

WebSocket reuse metadata probe:

```sh
cargo run -p harness-cli -- experiment ws-reuse-metadata --norotate
```

This live probe allows only one new WebSocket connection per minute, sends one request, then sends a
second request with changed logical session/thread/window/parent/subagent/turn metadata. If the
second request completes, those request-header changes did not require another handshake.

In the TUI, `/model 5.5 xhigh fast` selects `gpt-5.5`, extra-high reasoning, and Codex Fast mode.
The bottom status line begins with the active box, execution backend, and access mode, followed by
the session, provider, model settings, and context usage.

## Current TUI controls

- Type text to edit the input line.
- `Enter` submits the input to the harness and clears the input. While a response is active,
  `Enter` queues the input as steering instead of submitting it immediately, except slash commands
  beginning with `/` are sent to the runtime immediately.
- `Ctrl-J` or `Shift-Enter` inserts a newline in the input editor; terminal-reported
  `Shift-Enter` repeats insert repeated newlines.
- The input area starts at 3 rows and grows with multiline input up to 40% of the terminal height.
- The input area has a 2-column left margin with a guide line, prompt (`›`), and
  `▲`/`▼` overflow indicators.
- `Ctrl-A` and `Ctrl-E` move to the start/end of the current input line.
- `Left`, `Right`, `Home`, and `End` move the input cursor.
- `Ctrl-Backspace` or `Alt-Backspace` deletes the previous word.
- `Ctrl-Z` undoes the previous input edit; `Ctrl-Y` redoes it.
- `Ctrl-C` clears non-empty input. With empty input, the first `Ctrl-C` shows a yellow warning on
  the status line, and the second `Ctrl-C` exits.
- While a response is active, the unframed activity strip above the input shows
  `• Working (<elapsed>s • esc to interrupt)`. `Esc` interrupts instead of exiting in that state.
- Queued steering is shown in the same activity strip as
  `queued <message> (esc to steer instantly)`. `Esc` sends that queued steer immediately.
- When agents are present, the same unframed strip lists them without a frame; if the strip has more
  agents than available rows it ends with `and x more`.
- Assistant text streams into the transcript as `response.output_text.delta` frames arrive.
- Transcript entries use compact muted markers (`•` for assistant, `»` for input), subtle
  assistant/input text shades, and wrapped long lines; tool blocks keep their syntax highlighting
  behind a compact tool marker.
- `PageUp`/`PageDown` or the mouse wheel scroll the transcript without editing input; `Ctrl-Home`
  jumps to the oldest retained transcript line and `Ctrl-End` returns to live tail follow mode.
  New transcript output autoscrolls while the view is at the tail and preserves the current view
  while scrolled up. A vertical scrollbar is shown when retained transcript content exceeds the
  visible transcript area.
- The TUI renders only the visible transcript viewport and keeps a bounded in-memory transcript tail
  instead of retaining the entire session log. Durable session history remains in the snapshot-plus-
  journal session store.

- The bottom status line marks an active stream with `● active` and shows `ttft: pending` until the
  first assistant text delta, then displays the measured TTFT in milliseconds.
- `/developer on` sends subsequent input as Responses `developer` messages. This is the default.
- `/developer off` sends subsequent input as Responses `user` messages.
- `/developer` toggles between developer and user input roles.
- `/edit` opens the persisted user/assistant message and native tool-call picker. `Enter` loads the
  selected message or exact native tool input into the prompt for editing. `Delete` removes any
  selected entry. Direct forms are `/edit <sequence> <replacement text>` and
  `/edit delete <sequence>`. Each change activates a new session fork, leaving the original session
  unchanged. Deleting a tool call also removes its correlated execution and result records.
- `/model <model> [reasoning] [tier]` updates the model settings for subsequent turns.
- `/persist [task|pause|continue]` toggles or controls automatic continuation for the previous or explicitly provided task
  until the model verifies completion criteria and calls the `mark_task_complete` custom tool. Run
  `/persist` again with no task to disable active persist mode. Use `/persist pause` to pause the loop without ending the current request, `/persist continue` to resume, or send another message/steering to resume. If a user interrupt is requested (e.g. via `Esc`), the persist loop is automatically paused.
- `Backspace` deletes the previous input character.
- Idle `Esc` or confirmed `Ctrl-C` exits the TUI and prints the session id for resume.

readme.text:
# COVID-19-Aufarbeitung: Forschungsbasis

Stand: 2026-05-17

Dieses Verzeichnis sammelt die Forschungsbasis fuer eine spaetere evidenzbasierte Aufarbeitung der COVID-19-Pandemie. Es ist bewusst kein finaler LaTeX-Report. Ziel ist eine nachvollziehbare Sammlung von Quellen, Claims, Gegenargumenten, Minderheitspositionen, methodischen Grenzen und spaeteren Neubewertungen.

## Arbeitsprinzipien

- Keine erfundenen Quellen, Zahlen, DOI-Nummern oder Zitate.
- Jede belastbare Aussage verweist auf eine Quellen-ID aus [sources/source_register.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/source_register.tsv).
- Widersprueche, fehlende Daten und methodische Schwachstellen werden ausdruecklich markiert.
- Minderheitspositionen werden fair dokumentiert, aber nach Evidenzqualitaet gewichtet.
- Politische Naehe, mediale Lautstaerke oder institutionelle Autoritaet ersetzen keine methodische Bewertung.
- Damaliger Wissensstand und heutige Evidenzlage werden getrennt dargestellt.

## Struktur

- [methodology/evidence_grading.md](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/methodology/evidence_grading.md): Bewertungsraster, Claim-Schema, Umgang mit Unsicherheit.
- [methodology/search_protocols.md](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/methodology/search_protocols.md): Suchbausteine, Einschluss-/Ausschlusskriterien und Screening-Protokoll.
- [sources/source_register.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/source_register.tsv): Quellenregister mit IDs, Typen, URLs und Notizen.
- [sources/source_urls.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/source_urls.tsv): Schlanke ID-zu-URL-Datei aus dem Quellenregister.
- [sources/all_source_urls.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/all_source_urls.tsv): Einheitlicher Source-ID-zu-URL-Lookup fuer `S...`-Quellen und `BTEE...`-Enquete-Ressourcen mit lokalen Pfaden.
- [sources/source_cache_manifest.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/source_cache_manifest.tsv): Lokaler Cache-/Zugriffsstatus aller registrierten URLs.
- [sources/no_btee_source_text_manifest.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/no_btee_source_text_manifest.tsv): Text-Extraktionsmanifest fuer 39 registrierte Quellen aus der no-BTEE-Anschlussqueue.
- [sources/source_text/2026-05-17/](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/source_text/2026-05-17): Lokale Text-Sidecars fuer die no-BTEE-Anschlussquellen.
- [sources/no_btee_linked_pdf_manifest.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/no_btee_linked_pdf_manifest.tsv): Manifest fuer vier aus Landing Pages verlinkte Full-PDFs zu WHO-Therapeutics, WHO-Clinical-Management und World-Bank-Collapse-and-Recovery inklusive Text-Sidecars.
- [sources/local_rki/](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/local_rki/README.md): Metadatenindex fuer den lokal bereitgestellten RKI-Files-Bundle S211-S215.
- [sources/link_check_notes_2026-05-17.md](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/sources/link_check_notes_2026-05-17.md): Linkcheck-Status und bekannte Zugriffscaveats.
- [matrices/research_questions.md](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/research_questions.md): Themen- und Fragestellungsmatrix.
- [matrices/screening_log_template.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/screening_log_template.tsv): Vorlage fuer systematische Screening-Logs.
- [matrices/systematic_search_registry.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/systematic_search_registry.tsv): Priorisierte Suchplanung mit Suchstrings, Datenbanken, Claim-Mapping und vorhandenen Source-IDs.
- [matrices/search_runs.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/search_runs.tsv): Operatives Suchlaufregister mit Status, Filtern, Ergebniszahl und Exportpfad je Suche.
- [matrices/screening_log.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/screening_log.tsv): Erstes Screening-/Backfill-Log fuer Kernquellen und kuenftige Suchtreffer.
- [matrices/claim_index.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/claim_index.tsv): Pruefbare Claims mit Perspektive, Evidenzrating, Quellen und Limitationen.
- [matrices/claim_notes_index.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/claim_notes_index.tsv): Index der narrativen Claim Notes mit Claim-, Kontroversen- und Source-IDs.
- [matrices/timeline_damals_heute.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/timeline_damals_heute.tsv): Datierte Matrix zu damaliger Plausibilitaet, spaeterer Evidenz und heutiger Gewichtung.
- [matrices/timeline_plausibel_vs_belegt.tsv](/Users/user/Developer/Developer/test/corona/matrices/timeline_plausibel_vs_belegt.tsv): Deutschsprachige, quellenbasierte Kompakt-Timeline "damals plausibel vs heute belegt" fuer zentrale Streitfelder.

readme.text:
# Fast React

Fast React is an experimental Rust-first implementation of React runtime
semantics with JavaScript package facades for the React ecosystem. The project
is building toward React-compatible behavior from the inside out: lanes,
fibers, update queues, hooks, effects, host boundaries, schedulers, test
renderers, and DOM integration are modeled behind conformance-backed gates
before any public compatibility claim is made.

The current compatibility target is React 19.2.6, including the published
`react`, `react-dom`, and related package surfaces.

## Project Status

Fast React is under active development and is not a drop-in replacement for
React today. Some direct package surfaces already expose React-shaped behavior,
while larger renderer paths remain deliberately private, diagnostic, or
fail-closed until they are proven by tests.

The project favors correctness evidence over broad claims:

- Published behavior is checked against React 19.2.6 runtime oracles.
- Internal Rust and JavaScript paths grow behind explicit private diagnostics.
- Public compatibility is only promoted when the relevant conformance gates are
  ready.
- Unsupported behavior should fail loudly instead of silently approximating
  React.

## What Is In This Repository

- `crates/fast-react-core` - renderer-agnostic React data structures such as
  lanes, fibers, flags, hook queues, effect rings, and context state.
- `crates/fast-react-reconciler` - root scheduling, begin/complete work,
  update queues, commit handoff diagnostics, hooks, context, and sync flushing.
- `crates/fast-react-host-config` - typed host capability boundaries and opaque
  host tokens.
- `crates/fast-react-test-renderer` - mutation host support and private
  test-renderer integration evidence.
- `crates/fast-react-napi` and `bindings/node` - placeholder native binding
  surfaces and transport diagnostics for future Node integration.
- `packages/react`, `packages/react-dom`, `packages/react-test-renderer`, and
  `packages/scheduler` - JavaScript package facades and compatibility gates.
- `tests/conformance` and `tests/benchmarks` - oracle, smoke, conformance, and
  benchmark admission tests.

Planning and accepted history live in `MASTER_PLAN.md` and
`MASTER_PROGRESS.md`.

## Getting Started

Requirements:

- Rust 1.95.0
- Node.js 26 or newer
- npm 11 or newer

Install dependencies:

```sh
npm ci --ignore-scripts
```

Run a quick package-surface smoke check:

```sh
npm run test:smoke
```

Run the JavaScript and conformance checks:

```sh
npm run check:js
```

Run the Rust test suite:

```sh
cargo test --workspace --all-features
```

Run the full workspace check:

```sh
npm run check
```

## Development Approach

Fast React uses React 19.2.6 as the behavioral reference. Source inspection is
used for internal model research, while public behavior is validated with
black-box runtime probes and checked-in oracle artifacts.

The implementation is intentionally incremental. A feature usually starts as a
private diagnostic that records the exact boundary shape, ordering, metadata,
or failure mode needed by a future public path. Only after the supporting
runtime, renderer, and conformance coverage are in place should that behavior
be treated as public compatibility.

This keeps the project honest: incomplete renderer behavior stays blocked, but
the underlying architecture can still advance with precise evidence.

## Current Direction

The main objective is a minimal real root render, update, and unmount path. The
active development themes are:

- lane-backed priorities and root lane bookkeeping
- FiberRoot and HostRoot update flow
- function component rendering, hooks, context, and effects
- sync flush and act routing
- host config boundaries and mutation handoff
- test renderer serialization, query, act, and error surfaces
- React DOM root, hydration, event, form, resource, and controlled input
  behavior
- conformance and benchmark coverage before compatibility promotion

## Useful Commands

```sh
npm run test:smoke
npm run check:package-surface
npm run check:benchmarks
npm run test:conformance
npm run check:js
npm run check:rust
npm run check
cargo test --workspace --all-features
```

## Package Notes

The React package facade has its own notes in `packages/react/README.md`.
The native binding placeholder is documented in `bindings/node/README.md`.

## License

This workspace is currently `UNLICENSED`.

details.name: spotify-drm-report
details.description: Missing DRM Enforcement in Spotify’s Accesspoint API: Proof of Concept Report (2023)

readme.text:
# Missing DRM Enforcement in Spotify’s Accesspoint API: Proof of Concept Report

This report details a flaw in Spotify's Accesspoint API, which allows any user with a valid Spotify account to download and decrypt songs without any Digital Rights Management (DRM) enforcement.

This vulnerability was reported to Spotify both in January 2020 (by another researcher) and again by myself in August 2023. For more than 5 years no action has been taken to address or fix the issue.

After exhausting all responsible disclosure options, I feel it’s necessary to make this information public in the hope that it will finally prompt Spotify to take action and implement proper security measures.

## [Demo](https://youtu.be/adMpsinuZvU)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c21064e6-c902-4de9-a0d9-e9df769f1708

## [Proof of concept](./src/examples/download.ts)

## Report:

Spotifys Accesspoint api does not enforce any Digital Rights Management (DRM) system to request and decrypt songs, apart from requiring a valid Spotify account (free or premium).
This allows any spotify user to download and decrypt songs from Spotify without verifying the system's integrity via DRM.

The following report describes the process of downloading and decrypting songs from Spotify without using any DRM system:

1.  Connect to Spotifys Accesspoint tcp api
2.  Setup the transport layer encryption

    - generate random ephemeral Diffie–Hellman keys
    - send a ClientHello message with the ephemeral public key
    - wait for the APResponseMessage that contains the remote public key
    - calculate a shared Diffie–Hellman key via the ephemeral private key and the remote public key
    - use the previously sent ClientHello/APResponseMessage and the shared key to derive symmetric send/receive keys and a HMAC hash
    - sent the HMAC hash as ClientResponsePlaintext message
    - use the derived symmetric send/receive keys to setup Shannon ciphers for further communication

3.  Authentication

    - Authenticate by sending a ClientResponseEncrypted message with the username and password of a valid Spotify account (can be premium or free)
    - Wait for the APWelcome message to indicate successful authentication
    - send a MercuryRequest message with the following uri `hm://keymaster/token/authenticated?scope=playlist-read&client_id=65b708073fc0480ea92a077233ca87bd&device_id=00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` where client_id is the permanent client id of the official Spotify client and device_id is any random uuid
    - wait for the MercuryReply message that contains the ephemeral access token that is valid for 1 hour

4.  Download song

    - Send a HTTP request to the url `https://spclient.wg.spotify.com/metadata/4/track/<track_id>` with the ephemeral access token as the Authorization header and `track_id` of the desired track
    - The response JSON object has an array `file` with different URLs to download the track
    - Download the file with the desired bitrate and codec from one of the URLs
    - Note: The file urls are valid for a limited time and each file is encrypted with a different AES 128 CTR key
    - Note: free accounts can only download files with a maximum bitrate of 160kbps

5.  Decryption

    - Request the decryption key from the Accesspoint api by sending a RequestKey message with the `track_id` and `file_id` of the downloaded track
    - Wait for the KeyResponse message that contains the decryption key
    - Decrypt the downloaded file with the AES 128 CTR decryption key

The decrypted track can then be played with any media player that supports the codec of the downloaded file.

### Conclusion:

In contrary to the web player, which uses the Widevine DRM system to verify the integrity of the client and only allows playback of songs in the web player.
The Accesspoint/SPClient api does not use any DRM system to verify the integrity of the client.
The only necessary information to download and decrypt songs is the track id and a valid Spotify account, which can be registered for free by anyone.

readme.text: # React Native Skia List ![](./docs/static/img/banner.png) React Native Skia List is a high-performance list component for React Native. \ It is built on top of [@shopify/react-native-skia](https://shopify.github.io/react-native-skia/), a powerful 2D graphics library designed to be fast and customizable. ## Installation > [!CAUTION] > This library is in early development and not ready for production use. ```sh yarn add react-native-skia-list @shopify/react-native-skia react-native-keyboard-controller react-native-reanimated react-native-gesture-handler ``` ## [Documentation](https://samuelscheit.github.io/react-native-skia-list/) You can achieve good looking, interactive and high-performance lists with a lot of items like the following example: ## Usage ```tsx // needed for SkiaDomApi type import type {} from "@shopify/react-native-skia/lib/typescript/src/renderer/HostComponents"; import { Skia } from "@shopify/react-native-skia"; import { SkiaFlatList } from "react-native-skia-list"; import { useSafeAreaInsets } from "react-native-safe-area-context"; import { GestureHandlerRootView } from "react-native-gesture-handler"; import { KeyboardProvider } from "react-native-keyboard-controller"; // Create a Skia ParagraphBuilder that will be used to build the text for each item const paragraphBuilder = Skia.ParagraphBuilder.Make({ textStyle: { color: Skia.Color("black"), fontSize: 20, }, }); export default function Test() { const safeArea = useSafeAreaInsets(); return ( [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]} // To optimize performance for the initial mount you can provide a transformItem function // It will be called once for each item when it is mounted the first time transformItem={(item, index, id, state) => { "worklet"; paragraphBuilder.reset(); // reuses the paragraphBuilder for each item const text = `Item ${item}`; return paragraphBuilder.addText(text).build(); }} // renderItem will be called whenever an item visibility changes renderItem={(item, index, state, element) => { "worklet"; const { width } = state.layout.value; item.layout(width); // calculates the paragraph layout const height = item.getHeight(); // gets the height of the paragraph // element is a Skia.GroupNode or will be undefined if only the height of the element is needed if (!element) return height; element.addChild( // see the following link for all element types // https://github.com/Shopify/react-native-skia/blob/5c38b27d72cea9c158290adb7d23c6109369ac2f/packages/skia/src/renderer/HostComponents.ts#L72-L191 SkiaDomApi.ParagraphNode({ paragraph: item, x: 0, y: 0, width, }) ); return height; }} /> ); } ``` ## Contributing See the [contributing guide](https://github.com/SamuelScheit/react-native-skia-list/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) to learn how to contribute to the repository and the development workflow. ## License MIT

pullRequests.title: Fix cargo-chef cook inputs for path dependencies
pullRequests.body:
### Motivation
- `cargo chef cook` was failing to resolve local path dependencies (error reading `/api/Cargo.toml`) because the builder stage did not include the crate manifests used by path deps, so the dependency cooking step needed the real `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` inputs.

### Description
- Introduce a `planner` stage that copies the service and local crate directories and runs `cargo chef prepare` to generate a `recipe.json` for each service.
- Add a `builder` stage which copies the generated `recipe.json` and the `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` files for `shared`, `api`, `database`, and the target service into `/app` so `cargo chef cook` can resolve path dependencies.
- Ensure `WORKDIR` is set to the service directory and run `cargo chef cook --recipe-path /app/<service>/recipe.json` with cache mounts, then copy real sources and run the final `cargo build` to produce the service binary.
- Keep the runtime stage unchanged aside from sourcing the built binary from the `builder` stage into the final image.

### Testing
- No automated tests were run for these Dockerfile changes.

pullRequests.title: Refine cargo-chef Docker stages for Rust builds
pullRequests.body:
### Motivation
- Improve Docker build caching reliability for Rust services by adopting the canonical `cargo-chef` planner/builder flow. 
- Remove the fragile placeholder-source approach so dependency cooking is derived from a `recipe.json` instead of synthetic files.

### Description
- Update `platform/Dockerfile` and `scraper/Dockerfile` to introduce a `chef` base stage, a `planner` stage that copies crate directories and runs `cargo chef prepare --recipe-path recipe.json`, and a `builder` stage that copies the generated recipe and runs `cargo chef cook --release --recipe-path /app/<service>/recipe.json` with cache mounts for the cargo registry, git, and `target` directories. 
- Remove placeholder source generation and `touch` invalidation steps and instead `COPY` real sources after cooking dependencies, then run `cargo build --release --locked -p <package>` and `cp` the built binary to `/tmp` for the runtime image to consume. 
- Preserve runtime images using `debian:bookworm-slim` that install only runtime dependencies and copy the final binary from the `builder` stage. 
- Use explicit recipe paths in `cargo chef cook` invocations and maintain cache mount IDs (`*-cargo`, `*-cargo-git`, `*-target`) to improve layer caching.

### Testing
- No automated tests were run for these Dockerfile changes.

readme.text:
# Technical analysis of browser fingerprinting techniques based on FingerprintJS

## [Paper](./paper/paper.pdf)

Authors:
[Samuel Scheit](https://samuelscheit.com/),
[James Bergfeld](mailto:j.bergfeld@tum.de)

## Abstract

This work provides a comprehensive technical analysis of browser fingerprinting techniques, in particular using FingerprintJS. Browser fingerprinting allows individual users to be identified based on specific characteristics of their web browser without the need for cookies or other traditional tracking methods. This study examines the various components and mechanisms of FingerprintJS in detail, including their ability to create unique fingerprints and evaluate their accuracy and reliability. In addition, the effectiveness of these fingerprinting techniques in various application scenarios is analyzed and evaluated.

A central part of this research is the development of a custom fingerprinting library and the collection of our own dataset to validate and evaluate the methods. By analyzing this dataset, additional insights into the practical challenges and performance of the fingerprinting methods could be gained. The goal is to highlight the strengths and weaknesses of the current methods and to identify possible improvements and possible fingerprinting countermeasures.

## General

-   [demo/](./demo) Contains a POC with the fingerprint.pro.js library that can be run locally.

-   [notes/](./notes) Contains notes and assets for documentation.

-   [paper/](./paper) Contains the paper in typst with all assets.

-   [overrides](./overrides) Contains the browser overrides (JS source files) to debug the [FingerprintJS demo](https://fingerprint.com/demo/).

-   [website](./website) Contains the [website](https://fingerprint.samuelscheit.com/) with the custom fingerprinting library.

readme.text:
# openwebui-gateway

A FastAPI proxy that exposes an Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint in front of an Open WebUI instance, so Claude Code CLI can use your Open WebUI models without a paid Anthropic API key.

```
Claude Code CLI  →  openwebui-gateway  →  Open WebUI  →  LiteLLM / Vertex AI
```

## Quick start

```bash
cp .env.example .env
# Fill in OPENWEBUI_TOKEN (and optionally OPENWEBUI_BASE_URL)
docker compose up -d
```

The gateway listens on port **11434** by default (matches Ollama's port so existing tooling just works).

## Configuration

Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set the variables you need:

| Variable | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `OPENWEBUI_TOKEN` | Yes | Bearer token from Open WebUI → Settings → API Keys |
| `OPENWEBUI_BASE_URL` | No | Base URL of your Open WebUI instance (default: `https://ai-chat.app.iu-it.org`) |
| `OPENWEBUI_OAUTH_SESSION` | No | OAuth/SSO session cookie |
| `OPENWEBUI_AFFINITY` | No | Load-balancer affinity cookie |
| `API_KEY` | No | Protect this gateway with a key; leave empty for open access |
| `PORT` | No | Port to listen on (default: `8080` inside Docker, exposed as `11434`) |
| `DIRECT_API_PROXY` | No | Proxy URL for direct OpenAI/Anthropic passthrough calls only, e.g. `socks5://127.0.0.1:9050` |
| `ANTHROPIC_MODEL_MAP` | No | Comma-separated `anthropic_name:upstream_name` pairs for model name translation |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` | No | Upstream model to use when the requested name can't be resolved |
| `ANTHROPIC_FORWARD_REASONING_EFFORT` | No | Forward Claude Code's `output_config.effort` to the upstream as OpenAI `reasoning_effort` (`low`/`medium`/`high`; `xhigh`/`max` clamp to `high`). Default on; set to `0` to disable |

### Model resolution

When Claude Code requests a model (e.g. `claude-opus-4-7`), the gateway resolves it in order:

1. Exact match in `ANTHROPIC_MODEL_MAP`
2. Exact match in the upstream catalog
3. Date-suffix stripped (e.g. `claude-opus-4-5-20250929` → `claude-opus-4-5`)
4. `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` fallback

## Using with Claude Code CLI

Point Claude Code at the gateway by setting two environment variables:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434
```

### Shell functions for easy mode switching

Add these to your `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc` to switch between gateway and paid API:

```bash
# Gateway mode — routes through openwebui-gateway; shows [gw] in prompt
claude-gw() {
  local old_ps1="$PS1"
  export PS1="[gw] $PS1"
  echo "[ openwebui-gateway @ http://localhost:11434 ]"
  ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:11434" \
    command claude "$@"
  export PS1="$old_ps1"
}

# Paid API mode — direct Anthropic (uses your real ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
claude-paid() {
  echo "[ Anthropic API (paid) ]"
  unset ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL
  command claude "$@"
}
```

Then reload: `source ~/.bashrc`

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `claude-gw` | Claude Code via gateway; prompt prefixed with `[gw]` while session is active |
| `claude-paid` | Claude Code via direct Anthropic API |

To make the gateway the default when you just type `claude`:

```bash
alias claude='claude-gw'
```

## Using with Codex CLI

The gateway speaks the OpenAI Responses API, so [Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex) can use it as a drop-in provider. Codex CLI 0.128+ requires the Responses API, so make sure your gateway container exposes `/v1/responses` — rebuild if you're on an older image:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

Drop this into `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
model = "gpt-5.5"
model_provider = "openwebui"

[model_providers.openwebui]
name = "openwebui-gateway"
base_url = "http://localhost:11434/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
env_key = "OPENWEBUI_GATEWAY_KEY"
```

Then run Codex through the gateway:

```bash
# Gateway mode — routes Codex through openwebui-gateway
codex-gw() {
  echo "[ openwebui-gateway @ http://localhost:11434 ]"
  OPENWEBUI_GATEWAY_KEY="${API_KEY:-dummy}" \
    command codex "$@"
}
```

If you set `API_KEY` in the gateway's `.env`, export the matching value into `OPENWEBUI_GATEWAY_KEY` (the helper above picks it up automatically when `API_KEY` is in your shell env). If `API_KEY` is empty in the gateway, any non-empty value works.

Pick any model name your upstream catalog or `ANTHROPIC_MODEL_MAP` resolves — `gpt-5.5` above assumes it's in the catalog.

## Direct provider passthrough

The gateway can also proxy native OpenAI and Anthropic API calls directly to the
providers. These routes do not use Open WebUI, do not translate request or
response schemas, and still require the gateway `API_KEY` when one is configured.
For direct provider calls, send the gateway key as `x-gateway-api-key` so the
provider SDK can keep using its normal auth headers.

```bash
# OpenAI SDKs: appends /chat/completions, /responses, /models, etc. under /v1
export OPENAI_BASE_URL="http://localhost:11434/direct/openai/$OPENAI_API_KEY/v1"

# Anthropic SDKs: appends /v1/messages, /v1/messages/count_tokens, etc.
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:11434/direct/anthropic/$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
```

To route only these direct provider calls through a proxy such as Tor:

```bash
export DIRECT_API_PROXY="socks5://127.0.0.1:9050"
```

Provider keys in URLs can be captured by shell history, access logs, browser
history, and reverse proxies. Use the direct routes only where that tradeoff is
acceptable.

## Analytics

The gateway records every request to a SQLite database. View the dashboard:

```
http://localhost:11434/analytics
```

## Development

```bash
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
pytest
```

Run locally without Docker:

```bash
uvicorn app:app --reload --port 11434
```

## Summary

Reconstruct `response.completed.output` from preceding `response.output_item.done` events for streamed HTTP Responses requests.

The merge helper now lives in `routing_core`, so the HTTP and WebSocket paths share one implementation.

## Root cause

The Codex WebSocket backend can emit completed output items before a terminal `response.completed` event whose `output` is empty. The HTTP gateway forwarded that empty terminal event unchanged, so streaming SDK consumers persisted no usable result.

## Validation

- `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_routing_core.py tests/test_responses_websocket.py tests/test_app_responses.py tests/test_codex_api.py -q`

# Myrodex.gg

This repository is a Bun workspace monorepo. The main Next.js app lives in `apps/myrodex`.
The backoffice Next.js app lives in `apps/backoffice` and reuses shared auth, Drizzle, users, sponsor, and entity modules from `apps/myrodex`.

## Setup

Setup a postgres database [here](https://www.postgresql.org/download/).

Execute the following command in the terminal to open the postgres shell:

```
psql -h localhost -p 5432 -d postgres
```

then execute the following commands to create a database and user for myrodex:

```
CREATE DATABASE myrodex;
CREATE USER myrodex WITH ENCRYPTED PASSWORD 'lffwMR7ssPwGGL5p92';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE myrodex TO myrodex;
ALTER DATABASE myrodex OWNER TO myrodex;

CREATE DATABASE myrodex_backoffice;
CREATE USER myrodex_backoffice WITH ENCRYPTED PASSWORD 'lffwMR7ssPwGGL5p92';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE myrodex_backoffice TO myrodex_backoffice;
ALTER DATABASE myrodex_backoffice OWNER TO myrodex_backoffice;

```

## Create .env file

Create `apps/myrodex/.env` and add the following environment variables:

```
BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=3hlYn7uOQkH4xxgxQfsT8nlOqjjrgBZ9
DATABASE_URL=postgres://myrodex:lffwMR7ssPwGGL5p92@localhost:5432/myrodex
DRIZZLE_STUDIO_PASSWORD=lffwMR7ssPwGGL5p92
NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000
BETTER_AUTH_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000
```

Same for backoffice `apps/backoffice/.env`

```
BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=3hlYn7uOQkH4xxgxQfsT8nlOqjjrgBZ9
DATABASE_URL=postgres://myrodex_backoffice:lffwMR7ssPwGGL5p92@localhost:5432/myrodex_backoffice
DRIZZLE_STUDIO_PASSWORD=lffwMR7ssPwGGL5p92
NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000
BETTER_AUTH_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000
```

## Install bun + dependencies

Install Bun `1.3.13` from [here](https://bun.sh/).

then execute the following command from the repository root to install dependencies:

```
bun install
```

## Initialize the database

Execute the following command from the repository root to initialize the database:

```
bun run migrations:apply
```

For a separate backoffice database, create `apps/backoffice/.env` with its own
`DATABASE_URL`, then initialize that database with:

```
bun run migrations:backoffice:apply
```

Backoffice owns its application tables directly and mirrors the shared Myrodex
runtime schema with generated reconciliation migrations. Applying migrations
also validates shared tables, columns, and enum values before the app starts.

## Run the development server

Execute the following command from the repository root to run the development server:

```
bun dev
```

To run the backoffice app locally:

```
bun run dev:backoffice
```

## Documentation

- [Deployment](docs/deployment.md)
- [Stripe billing and organization exports](docs/billing.md)
- [Backoffice Partner CRM](docs/backoffice-partners.md)
- [Backoffice → personal Microsoft 365 contacts](docs/backoffice-m365-personal-contacts.md)

## Summary

Builds Customizable Home Dashboard V1 for `apps/myrodex`:

- Replaces the `/` home chat with a customizable dashboard backed by `dashboard_layouts` persistence.
- Adds user layout save/load/reset and organization default save routes with explicit auth checks.
- Adds a stable widget registry, layout sanitizer, data shaping, and loaders for counts, lists, spotlights, quick actions, alerts, and next actions using existing access helpers and existing entities.
- Adds drag/drop and resize with `react-grid-layout`, Recharts trend rendering through the existing chart theme helpers, shadcn UI, and lucide icons.
- Defers fake match result analytics: no winrate, trophy/skull result lists, or prize-result semantics are introduced.

## Root Cause / Design Notes

Dashboard layouts need their own user-scoped persistence instead of generic CRUD so a user override cannot become an organization-wide layout by accident. Widget visibility and saved layouts are sanitized on load/save from the registry permissions. Planner dashboard access keeps root-admin bypass separate from org-admin organization scoping to avoid cross-organization planner leakage.

## Validation

- `bun test apps/myrodex/lib/dashboard/registry.test.ts` - 8 pass
- `bun --cwd apps/myrodex test:e2e:dev --grep "customizable dashboard"` - 5 pass
- `bun --cwd apps/myrodex lint` - exits 0 with existing warnings
- `bun --cwd apps/myrodex tsc --noEmit --pretty false` - exits 2 from existing unrelated table/custom-field/test typing issues; filtered dashboard diagnostics are empty

No match schema, match route, or match save-flow files are changed. Production E2E/build remains blocked by the existing non-dashboard TypeScript failures unless CI ignores those checks.

pullRequests.title: [codex] Implement Myro AI operator foundation
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Implements the Myro AI operator foundation behind `/api/myro` with provider-neutral orchestration, streamed responses, persisted assistant messages, and a narrow policy-controlled tool layer over existing CRUD/read services.

This PR intentionally targets `codex/customizable-home-dashboard-v1` instead of `origin/main` because the remote default branch is stale relative to the local monorepo baseline. The base branch was pushed separately so the Myro diff stays scoped to the AI operator work.

## Root cause

Chat messages previously inferred assistant/user display state from whether the sender matched the current user. That made any non-current human user render as `assistant`, which would collide with real bot semantics. This change persists explicit message author roles and assistant metadata so human and AI-authored messages are distinguishable at the data boundary.

## What changed

- Adds `authorRole` and `assistantMetadata` to persisted chat messages with a migration.
- Adds a pure chat record mapper that preserves human vs assistant semantics.
- Updates dashboard chat to call `/api/myro` in Myro mode and stream SSE results.
- Adds Myro orchestration with optional `MYRO_LLM_ENDPOINT` / `MYRO_LLM_API_KEY` and fallback tool planning.
- Adds Myro tools for search, context reads, mutation proposals/execution, notifications, and activity summaries with sensitive-field blocking and managed-field stripping.
- Enforces operation-specific mutation preparation so creates cannot become updates and update/delete proposals require IDs.
- Persists assistant metadata for proposals, tool traces, citations, and confidence.

## Validation

- `bun test lib/chat/message-record.test.ts lib/chat/message-thread.test.ts lib/myro/tools.test.ts`
- `bun --cwd apps/myrodex build`
- `bun --cwd apps/myrodex lint` passes with existing warnings and no errors.

A full `bun test` run still picks up Playwright e2e specs under Bun and exposes existing insight test setup failures (`ReferenceError: Cannot access 'db' before initialization`), so the focused Myro/chat tests above were used for this scoped PR.

pullRequests.title: Move sponsor deals to dedicated page; add deal editor and price upsert
pullRequests.body:
### Motivation
- Decouple sponsor deals from the Sponsor details sheet so deals can be managed on their own page and edited with a consistent `DataDisplay` flow.
- Provide a reusable deal editor component so deals can be created/edited in a sheet or on a dedicated deal details page.
- Support sending `price` objects when creating/updating deals and ensure prices are upserted server-side so the UI can show/edit monetary values per currency.

### Description
- Replace inline Deals tab in the sponsor details view with a link to a dedicated deals page by updating `app/(dashboard)/sponsors/[sponsorId]/SponsorDetailsContent.tsx` to show a `Deals` navigation button instead of rendering the table inline.
- Add a client-side reusable deal editor component `DealDetailsContent` at `app/(dashboard)/sponsors/[sponsorId]/deals/DealDetailsContent.tsx` that handles view/create/edit flows with `useDetails` and `DataTableAction` and supports editing `price` objects and dates via `DatePicker`.
- Add a sponsor deals list page component `SponsorDealsContent` at `app/(dashboard)/sponsors/[sponsorId]/deals/SponsorDealsContent.tsx` that renders deals using `DataDisplay` and wires the sheet editor to `DealDetailsContent`.
- Add route pages for the deals listing and individual deal details: `app/(dashboard)/sponsors/[sponsorId]/deals/page.tsx` and `app/(dashboard)/sponsors/[sponsorId]/deals/[dealId]/page.tsx` with a small client wrapper `SponsorDealDetailsPage` to fetch deal from `SponsorContext` and render `DealDetailsContent`.
- Extend the DB/Zod update schema so sponsor deals can accept a `price` object by importing `pricesUpdateSchema` and changing `sponsorDealsUpdateSchema` to `.and(z.object({ price: pricesUpdateSchema.optional() }))` in `lib/db/schema/sponsors.ts`.

# archive

Kinoger reverse-engineered API built with Bun.

## Install

bun install

## Run

bun run dev

Server default:

http://localhost:3000

Production container:

`docker build -t kinoger-api .`

The Jellyfin plugin can configure an optional playback CDN proxy. HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS4,
SOCKS4a, SOCKS5, and SOCKS5h proxy URLs are supported. When configured, the proxy is applied
to external-provider handshakes, HLS manifests, keys, segments, validation probes, and direct
MP4 range requests. This keeps IP-bound provider signatures valid. A failed configured proxy is
never bypassed; leaving the setting blank enables direct CDN access.

Persist `/app/tmp` if download jobs should survive container replacement. Jellyfin and this API should share a private Docker network under the hostname `kinoger-api`.

Open the UI at:

http://localhost:3000/

Direct `fetch` is attempted first for every Kinoger page request.
Patchright is only used as a fallback when Kinoger responds with a Cloudflare challenge page such as `403`, `Just a moment...`, or similar clearance/wait screens.

The browser fallback now stops the page once the HTML is ready, and only keeps waiting when it still detects an active Cloudflare challenge.

Patchright defaults to headed mode for Cloudflare/Turnstile handling.
Set `KINOGER_PATCHRIGHT_HEADLESS=true` if you explicitly want headless mode.

## Endpoints

GET /health

GET /catalog

GET /playback/master.m3u8?url=https://kinoger.com/stream/21169-unmoralische-geschichten-stream.html

GET /resolve?url=https://kinoger.com/stream/10875-doctor-strange-in-the-multiverse-of-madness-stream-deut.html

GET /resolve?url=https://kinoger.com/stream/8213-the-orville-stream.html&season=1&episode=1

GET /resolve?p2pId=tznac

GET /resolve/p2p/tznac

GET /search?query=the+orville

GET /series?url=https://kinoger.com/stream/8213-the-orville-stream.html

GET /downloads

POST /downloads

GET /download-files/:jobId/archive.zip

Optional query:

includeInfo=true

This adds decrypted output from /api/v1/info in addition to /api/v1/video.

For pages with multiple episodes, `/resolve` now requires `season` and `episode`.
For single-entry pages such as movies, `/resolve?url=...` auto-selects that one entry.
Optional `provider=...` overrides the default provider choice. Without it, the API prefers a p2p-backed provider when available.

`/series` returns the full provider matrix for the page. Movies are normalized into one season with one episode so the UI and download flow can handle shows and movies with the same shape.

`/playback/info` resolves and validates the selected provider, calculates the duration of finite HLS VOD playlists, and caches the provider URL plus the complete validated playlist graph for thirty minutes. Concurrent requests for the same episode share one resolution. `/playback/media` then reuses that result to start immediately, keeps provider headers inside the API, coalesces repeated immutable fragment requests, and advertises MPEG-TS and fragmented MP4 resources with their real media types. Optional `season`, `episode`, and `target=cf|source|tiktok` parameters use the same selection rules as `/resolve`.

`/downloads` creates background jobs that resolve the selected title/season/episode, fetch the HLS playlists and segments, and write a zip archive containing the local `.m3u8` files plus the downloaded `.ts`/`.m4s` segment bundle. No ffmpeg merge/transcode step is used.

## Cloudflare/Cookie

If Kinoger returns 403, pass a valid cookie to this API:

Header:

x-kinoger-cookie: PHPSESSID=...

Or environment variable:

KINOGER_COOKIE="PHPSESSID=..."

## Example

curl "http://localhost:3000/resolve?url=https://kinoger.com/stream/10875-doctor-strange-in-the-multiverse-of-madness-stream-deut.html"

curl "http://localhost:3000/resolve?url=https://kinoger.com/stream/8213-the-orville-stream.html&season=1&episode=1"

curl "http://localhost:3000/resolve?p2pId=tznac"

curl "http://localhost:3000/resolve/p2p/tznac?includeInfo=true"

curl "http://localhost:3000/search?query=the+orville"

curl "http://localhost:3000/series?url=https://kinoger.com/stream/8213-the-orville-stream.html"

curl "http://localhost:3000/downloads"

curl -X POST "http://localhost:3000/downloads" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "url": "https://kinoger.com/stream/8213-the-orville-stream.html",
    "scope": "episode",
    "seasonNumber": 1,
    "episodeNumber": 5
  }'

## P2P probe

The repository now includes a standalone Bun script that:

- resolves a Kinoger stream URL, or
- loads a cached payload from `src/result.json`

It then derives the tracker swarm identity from `video.swarmId`, joins the configured WebSocket trackers with Node-side WebRTC, and logs peer discovery and connection events.

Run from cached data:

`bun run probe:p2p -- --result src/result.json --timeout-ms 15000`

Resolve live first:

`bun run probe:p2p -- --url https://kinoger.com/stream/8213-the-orville-stream.html --timeout-ms 15000`

Optional flags:

- `--cookie "PHPSESSID=..."`
- `--include-info`
- `--stream-type main|secondary`
- `--stream-index 0`

This is only a connection probe. It does not implement the segment exchange protocol on top of the data channel.

## HLS fetch

The repository also includes a direct HLS fetch script that reads `video.source` from the resolved payload, fetches the master playlist, selects a variant, and downloads the first N segments.

Run from cached data:

`bun run hls:fetch -- --result src/result.json --segments 3`

Fetch the `video.cf` target instead of `video.source`:

`bun run hls:fetch -- --result src/result.json --target cf --segments 3`

Fetch the TikTok-backed target:

`bun run hls:fetch -- --result src/result.json --target tiktok --segments 3`

Alias:

`bun run hls:fetch -- --result src/result.json --context tiktok --segments 3`

Resolve a fresh payload first:

`bun run hls:fetch -- --url https://kinoger.com/stream/8213-the-orville-stream.html --segments 3`

Optional flags:

- `--output-dir /absolute/path`
- `--target source|cf|tiktok`
- `--variant-index 0`
- `--season 1 --episode 1` for multi-episode pages
- `--cookie "PHPSESSID=..."`
- `--include-info`

The fetcher auto-detects which origin/referer context to use for the selected target.

Resolved Kinoger payloads also include `requestContextHints` describing which origin/referer pair should be used for each delivery target.
